title: The Tao that can be told
word: The Tao that can be told
hook: the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao; the nameless is the origin (Tao Te Ching 1)
carry: not the one that can be told

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old master wrote his book at a border gate, and your line was at the gate. Did you catch a threshold or two? Today we step through, into chapter one. Day one thousand sixty-three.

How would you describe the taste of water to someone who had never had any? Cool, maybe. Wet. Plain. Every word slides off it. Or the smell of rain on a hot sidewalk, or the face of someone you love. You can talk about these things for an hour and still not have handed them over. The words point. They don't arrive. The Tao Te Ching doesn't open by telling you what it's about. It opens by warning you that what it's about can't be fully told, and that the moment you've said it, you've already missed it a little.
screen: `THE TASTE OF WATER.` → `THE WORDS POINT. THEY DON'T ARRIVE.` → `A BOOK THAT BEGINS WITH A WARNING.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name." Notice Legge's word, trodden. In Chinese the line opens with one character used twice, first as a noun and then as a verb, the Tao that can be Tao'd, and that character can mean a road and can also mean to say. Legge chose the road, a way you can walk. Other translators choose the speaking, a way you can tell. Both readings stand side by side, and the line makes sense either way: any Tao you can map or describe is not the whole of it. Second, the nameless and the named. The chapter goes on to say that, thought of as having no name, the Tao is the origin of heaven and earth, and thought of as having a name, it is the mother of all things. Two faces of one thing. The nameless is where everything comes from. The named is where we live: kitchens, cities, words for every tree. Third, both are the same. The chapter says these two come from one source and only get different names as things unfold. It doesn't ask you to throw words away. It asks you to remember that every name is a small door into something larger than the name. Fourth, the mystery has a gate. The chapter ends by calling the deepest point of this mystery a gate, the way in to all that is subtle and wonderful. A gate again. The book written at a gate opens with one.
screen: `TRODDEN, OR SPOKEN?` · `THE NAMELESS AND THE NAMED.` · `ONE SOURCE, TWO NAMES.` · `THE MYSTERY HAS A GATE.` · then, large: `NOT THE ONE THAT CAN BE TOLD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit with something you can't name. Settle, and breathe. Look around for anything ordinary: a cup, a leaf, your own hand. Name it once, quietly. Cup. Then keep looking, past the name. The color where the light hits it. The weight of it in the air. The small shadow underneath. Each time a new word comes, let it go, and keep looking at what's still there after the words run out. If you pray, you can rest in what can't be named. If you don't, just stay with the looking. The bell holds the time.
The Tao that can be told. The opening line of the Tao Te Ching, which says that any way you can tread or tell is not the enduring Tao. Today's word.
screen: `THE TAO THAT CAN BE TOLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not the one that can be told. Today, when you name something quickly, a person, a mood, a day, add silently: and more than that. Day one thousand sixty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching return to its opening chapter again and again, and some Taoist teachers treat it as a reminder that every description of the Way falls short of the Way itself.

fork.setup: someone asks the old master to explain the Tao in one clear sentence. what does chapter one do?
options: say that the Tao that can be told is not the enduring Tao.
refuse to say anything at all.
fork.reveal: it speaks, and in the same breath warns that what it speaks of is more than the words. then it keeps going for the rest of the book.

original.note: Chinese, wú míng: no name, nameless. Chapter one says the nameless is the origin of heaven and earth.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Tao that can be told is a riddle meant to confuse.

what a scholar hears: the line uses one character twice, as a noun and a verb; Legge read the verb as trodden, others as spoken.

notes: Legge's opening two sentences quoted; please verify against the 1891 Sacred Books of the East text.
The double sense of 道 (a way; to speak) is stated from standard usage; Legge's 'trodden' versus 'spoken' in other translations is the point. Confirm phrasing.
Rest of the chapter paraphrased (nameless as Originator, named as Mother, the two the same, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful).
Day 1028 quoted the same Legge line with William James's ineffability; this day takes the trodden/told double reading, the nameless and named, and the gate image instead.
